body.objective: Students will be able to record MIDI parts.
successCriteria: I can record MIDI parts with a keyboard or step input
I can edit notes, quantize and adjust velocity
I can assign virtual instruments and balance a short arrangement
body.hook: A MIDI file doesn't contain any sound at all. It's a list of instructions: which note, how hard, how long. That's why the same MIDI part can become a grand piano, a string section or a synth with one click.

study.title: Notes Without Sound
study.question: How do producers use MIDI to build arrangements?
study.passage:
Tools: a DAW (GarageBand, BandLab, Soundtrap or similar) and a MIDI keyboard or the on-screen keyboard.
Part 1, What MIDI is (5 minutes): MIDI stores note number (pitch), velocity (1–127), start time and length. No audio.
Part 2, Record (15 minutes): Set a metronome at 90 bpm and a one-bar count-in. Record a four-bar chord part (C-G-Am-F) on a piano instrument. Then record a bass line on a new track.
Part 3, Edit (15 minutes): Open the piano roll. Fix wrong notes by dragging. Quantize to 1/8 notes (try 75% strength to keep some feel). Raise velocity on beat 1 of each bar for accent.
Part 4, Swap sounds (5 minutes): Change the chord track from piano to strings, then to a synth pad. Notice the same notes sound completely different.
Part 5, Drums and mix (10 minutes): Program a drum pattern in step input (kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats on eighths). Balance levels: drums and bass firm, chords lower, melody clear. Pan hi-hats slightly.

practice.q: Why might fully quantized drums sound robotic?
practice.a: Every hit is perfectly on the grid with the same velocity.

practice.q: How does changing an instrument change the mood?
practice.a: Different timbres create different feelings from the same notes.

practice.q: What should be loudest in most mixes?
practice.a: The melody or lead, with firm drums and bass.

practice.q: Why vary velocity in a hi-hat pattern?
practice.a: It sounds more human and creates groove.
